code --install-extension ./comment-doc-links-0.1.0.vsix

If you don't know the exact filename:

code --install-extension "$(ls *.vsix | head -1)"

Then verify:

code --list-extensions | grep comment

===============================================
So we're no longer looking at the earlier 0.1.0 state. The latest main includes the additional CRLF/CR handling, command guards, completion fixes, and the expanded E2E coverage.

Current state

I would now consider the extension technically ready for a Marketplace release candidate.

The important pieces are all present:

Two-way source ↔ Markdown navigation.
Exact anchor resolution.
Missing anchor does not prevent opening the target file.
Completion for source and Markdown references.
Diagnostics for provably broken references.
Workspace path traversal protection.
Block-comment handling.
CRLF and bare-CR handling.
Command-palette safety when commands receive invalid/missing arguments.
Unit + VS Code E2E tests.
VSIX packaging.
GitHub Actions CI on Node 20/22.
Marketplace metadata, icon, README, CHANGELOG and MIT license.

The final audit PR reports:

npm run lint       ✓
npm test           ✓ 66 unit tests
npm run test:e2e   ✓ 9 E2E tests
npm run package    ✓ VSIX builds

So the project has moved from prototype → release candidate.

One thing I would verify before publishing

There is one documentation/syntax detail worth consciously deciding.

The current implementation deliberately tolerates legacy Markdown forms:

## src/util/foo.js - anchor

and:

## src/util/foo.js#anchor

while the canonical syntax remains:

## src/util/foo.js — anchor

That tolerance is documented in the README/CHANGELOG and tested, so I would leave it as compatibility behavior, not remove it now. The current project has made that an intentional compatibility feature.

What remains

At this point I would not add more architecture or functionality.

The next phase is operational:

CURRENT
  │
  ├── Code ✓
  ├── Tests ✓
  ├── E2E ✓
  ├── CI ✓
  ├── VSIX ✓
  ├── README ✓
  ├── LICENSE ✓
  └── Marketplace metadata ✓
          │
          ▼
     RELEASE CANDIDATE
          │
          ├── Install generated VSIX locally
          ├── Test against your real production repo
          ├── Verify Marketplace metadata
          ├── Create GitHub release/tag
          └── Publish to VS Code Marketplace

One important distinction: the GitHub CI proves the automated test suite and packaging work, but it does not prove the extension behaves exactly as you expect inside your real repository. So I would make the next step a manual VSIX installation test against one of your actual repos before publishing.

Current GitHub main branch

where it is Install generated VSIX locally and how to install and how to Verify Marketplace metadata

Yes. These are two separate things:

Install the .vsix locally → test exactly what you're about to publish.
Verify Marketplace metadata → make sure package.json and the packaged extension will appear correctly in the VS Code Marketplace.
1. Where is the generated VSIX?

Your GitHub CI generates it here:

npx vsce package --no-dependencies

and uploads it as a GitHub Actions artifact named:

comment-doc-links-vsix

So the CI-generated .vsix is not currently committed to GitHub. It's an Actions artifact.

For local testing, I recommend generating one yourself.

From the extension repository:

npm ci
npm run lint
npm test
npm run test:e2e
npm run package

The last command:

npm run package

runs:

vsce package

and creates something like:

comment-doc-links-0.1.0.vsix

in the root of the extension repository.

Check:

ls -lh *.vsix
2. Install the VSIX into VS Code

You have two easy options.

Option A — VS Code UI

Open VS Code.

Go to:

Extensions

Then click the:

...

menu near the Extensions view.

Choose:

Install from VSIX...

Select:

comment-doc-links-0.1.0.vsix

VS Code will install it.

Then reload VS Code if prompted.

Option B — command line

From your extension repository:

code --install-extension ./comment-doc-links-0.1.0.vsix

If you don't know the exact filename:

code --install-extension "$(ls *.vsix | head -1)"

Then verify:

code --list-extensions | grep comment

You should see something corresponding to:

manish-sharma-getanchorio.comment-doc-links

The exact extension ID comes from:

publisher.name

Your current package.json has:

"name": "comment-doc-links",
"publisher": "manish-sharma-getanchorio"

so the expected ID is:

manish-sharma-getanchorio.comment-doc-links
3. Test the actual installed extension

This is important.

Don't test only inside the extension-development window.

Open one of your real application repositories in normal VS Code.

Then test:

Source → Markdown
// See documentation/claude/comments/ENC-74995.md#reconciliation-guarantee

Cmd/Ctrl-click it.

Expected:

ENC-74995.md
        ↓
reconciliation-guarantee
Markdown → source
## src/util/foo.js — reconciliation-guarantee

Cmd/Ctrl-click.

Expected:

foo.js
   ↓
matching source comment
Missing anchor

This is particularly important:

## src/util/foo.js — missing-anchor

If foo.js exists but missing-anchor doesn't:

Expected:

foo.js opens

not:

nothing happens
Missing file
## src/util/does-not-exist.js — anything

Expected:

diagnostic appears
navigation cannot open a nonexistent file.
4. Verify Marketplace metadata

There are actually two levels of verification.

Level 1 — Verify package.json

Your current metadata already contains the important Marketplace fields:

{
  "name": "comment-doc-links",
  "displayName": "Comment Doc Links",
  "description": "Navigate between source comments and markdown documentation with two-way links.",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "publisher": "manish-sharma-getanchorio",
  "license": "MIT",
  "repository": {
    "type": "git",
    "url": "https://github.com/anchor-os/commentDocLinksExtension"
  },
  "homepage": "https://github.com/anchor-os/commentDocLinksExtension",
  "bugs": {
    "url": "https://github.com/anchor-os/commentDocLinksExtension/issues"
  },
  "keywords": [...],
  "icon": "icon.png"
}

That's good.

5. Let vsce validate the package

This is the most useful local metadata check.

Run:

npx vsce ls

This shows what will actually be included in the VSIX.

Then:

npx vsce package

If vsce finds a packaging/manifest problem, it will report it.

You can also run:

npx vsce package --no-dependencies

which matches your CI packaging command.

6. Inspect the actual VSIX

A .vsix is basically a ZIP file.

Run:

unzip -l comment-doc-links-0.1.0.vsix

You should see important things such as:

extension/package.json
extension/README.md
extension/CHANGELOG.md
extension/LICENSE
extension/icon.png
extension/src/...

And you should not see things you don't want shipped, such as:

.git/
.github/
node_modules/
test fixtures/
.vscode/

depending on what your .vscodeignore excludes.

This is one of the best final checks before publishing.

7. Verify the Marketplace listing itself

You don't have a Marketplace listing until you publish it.

So you cannot currently verify the final public Marketplace page.

Before publishing, you can verify everything that will populate that page from package.json:

Marketplace field	Current source
Name	displayName
Description	description
Version	version
Publisher	publisher
Icon	icon
Categories	categories
Keywords	keywords
Repository	repository
Homepage	homepage
Issues	bugs
README	README.md
License	license
Changelog	CHANGELOG.md

Your current package.json has those core fields.

8. One thing we need before Marketplace publishing

You have:

"publisher": "manish-sharma-getanchorio"

That means the Marketplace publisher needs to exist and you need permission to publish under it.

If you haven't created the VS Code Marketplace publisher yet, you'll need to do that through the Visual Studio Marketplace publisher/account process.

Then you authenticate vsce and publish.

Don't run vsce publish yet.

First do:

npm run package

then:

code --install-extension ./comment-doc-links-0.1.0.vsix

test it against your real repo, and inspect:

npx vsce ls

and:

unzip -l comment-doc-links-0.1.0.vsix
